extracted.intended_audience: general readers, law students, journalists, and free-speech practitioners interested in First Amendment case law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and doctrinal standards governing when parody, satire, and other critical speech about public figures are protected by the First Amendment — as illustrated by the Hustler Magazine v. Falwell Supreme Court decision. Useful for evaluating whether a parody is actionable for libel or emotional-distress torts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody protection for public figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodies of public figures which could not reasonably be taken as true are protected against civil liability by the First Amendment, even if intended to cause emotional distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding of the case: an 8–0 Supreme Court decision protecting the Hustler parody ad (depicting Falwell in an incestuous, drunken scenario) because it could not reasonably be interpreted as stating actual facts about a public figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual malice standard for public-figure defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Amendment gives speakers immunity from sanction with respect to their speech concerning public figures unless their speech is both false and made with 'actual malice' — i.e., with knowledge of its falsehood or with reckless disregard for the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from New York Times Co. v. Sullivan; the Court applied this standard to speech-related tort claims concerning public figures and required falsity plus actual malice for liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot evade defamation limits via alternative torts
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional limits to defamation liability cannot be circumvented for claims arising from speech by asserting an alternative theory of tort liability such as intentional infliction of emotional distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court reversed a judgment that awarded damages under intentional infliction of emotional distress where the parody concerned a public figure and did not state provably false facts with actual malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity exclusion from First Amendment protection
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as the speech at issue is not 'obscene' and thus not subject to First Amendment protection, it should be subject to the actual-malice standard when it concerns public figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion distinguishes obscene material (unprotected) from parody/satire; if speech is obscene, First Amendment protections do not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 'outrageousness' as a sufficient basis for liability
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'outrageous' standard for awarding damages is impermissibly subjective and 'runs afoul' of the Court's refusal to permit damages because the speech may have an adverse emotional impact on the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court held that labeling speech 'outrageous' (i.e., because it causes emotional harm) cannot alone remove First Amendment protection; subjectivity of outrage makes it an unsuitable legal test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable-person test for parody interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody is protected where the communication 'could not reasonably be understood as describing actual facts' about the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At trial, the jury found and the district court held that the Hustler parody could not 'reasonably be understood' as asserting factual events about Falwell; that reasonable-understanding test was central to the libel ruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'public figure' for First Amendment cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Public figures are those 'intimately involved in the resolution of important public questions or, by reason of their fame, shape events in areas of concern to society at large.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Falwell was a televangelist and prominent political commentator, he was a public figure; thus higher First Amendment protections (actual malice) applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toleration of occasional false statements ('breathing space')
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Amendment tolerates occasional false statements because 'the breathing space that freedom of expression requires ... must tolerate occasional false statements' to avoid chilling constitutionally protected speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court's rationale: protecting even some false speech prevents an intolerable chilling effect on valuable public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody labeling and disclaimers (evidentiary, not dispositive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A publication's use of disclaimers or labeling (e.g., 'ad parody – not to be taken seriously', listing the piece as 'Fiction; Ad and Personality Parody') is part of the factual context but does not alone determine First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hustler ad included a small-print disclaimer and table-of-contents labeling; the Court's decision turned on broader doctrinal tests (reasonable interpretation, actual malice), not solely on the presence of a disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standard for private-figure defamation (Gertz)
rubrics_metrics.description: For private persons, the standard differs: 'actual malice' is not necessary for defamation of a private person if negligence is present (see Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references Gertz to note that public-figure standards (actual malice) do not automatically apply to private-person plaintiffs; different fault standards and remedies may obtain for private individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/genre-based protection for political cartoons and caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Political cartoons and caricature — often exploiting traits or embarrassing events and sometimes 'calculated to injure the feelings of the subject' — have historically been protected as part of robust political debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion cites Thomas Nast and historical examples to justify protecting satirical and critical forms of political expression even when they are biting or hurtful.
